questions.knowledge_point: Finding Equilibrium Points of a System
questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-3x(t)+4y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-6x(t)+8y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives an equation of the line in the phase space that contains all equilibrium points of the system above?
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ -6 & 8\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-3x+4y=0 \\ -6x+8y=0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the second equation is a multiple of the first one. So, we can disregard the second equation. 

From first equation, we get

$$
-3x+4y=0\,⇒\,4y=3x\,⇒\,y=\frac{3}{4}x.
$$

Therefore, the equilibrium points are given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}k \\ \frac{3}{4}k\end{aligned}],\,k\in R.
$$

This determines the line with the equation $y=\frac{3}{4}x.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Phase Portrait of a System With One Zero Eigenvalue
questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=6x(t)+2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=5,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are ${v}_{1}=[-1,\text{ }3]^{T}$ and ${v}_{2}=[1,\text{ }2]^{T},$ respectively. Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the system?

*Hint: Here, the dotted line represents the equilibrium solutions.*
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{5t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Let's now sketch the phase portrait.

- First, notice that ${x}_{E}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ are the equilibrium solutions of the system since ${x}_{E}^{′}(t)=0.$ These solutions form the line with the equation $y=-3x$ in the phase space, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14076166/assets/b39e589968babd6f1417b37dc0f53796ab363ee80ec5fc3860e9793b88b1e98c.png)

- Now, the line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 
$y=2x$
and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{5t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. Since ${e}^{5t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14076166/assets/12a1f8f11c3f1063804220884e6616ae4c9e9aee956adc575de1f0e88e0dd038.png)

All other non-equilibrium solutions are parallel to the vector ${v}_{2}.$ So, the phase portrait of our system looks as follows: 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14076166/assets/1b3ed684a9981397191fda952481ff10e114f5f092e83b3defa618c9c8d1cb46.png)

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Phase Portrait of a System With Repeated Zero Eigenvalue
questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-x(t)-y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=x(t)+y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvector corresponding to the only eigenvalue $\lambda =0$ of the system's matrix $A$ is $v=[-1,\text{ }1]^{T}.$ The vector $w=[1,\text{ }0]^{T}$ is such that $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$  Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the system?

*Hint: Here, the dotted line represents the equilibrium solutions.*
questions.worked_solution:
Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =0$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $v,$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

In our case, 

$$
\lambda =0,\,v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-t+1 \\ t\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that ${x}_{E}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ are equilibrium solutions of the system since ${x}_{E}^{′}(t)=0.$ These solutions form the line with the equation $y=-x$ in the phase space, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14076166/assets/9988933a3f4393f745b1df6f0dc667a4074f5ee787fab43fb392b117368a8ca9.png)

  

Now, we consider some general solutions of the form 

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-t+1 \\ t\end{aligned}].
$$

For example:

- When ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=1,$ we get the following curve: 

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-t \\ y=t+1\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add it to the phase space:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14076166/assets/2809f28b49c9782db6fdf3f5a8be7fd99ec6d9a08db8e81d91c4d6bc53efcdda.png)

- When ${c}_{1}=-1$ and ${c}_{2}=-1,$ we get the following curve: 

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=t \\ y=-t-1\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add it to the phase space:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14076166/assets/7fd67e8a768419dd497bc6345c5999ff921e6de492f60c5f217e93f8dc4d07c1.png)

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14076166/assets/dacab040d97838459bb9d0554ed08d09abd48f7716924fb3de2b52c1bf9cf556.png)

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Phase Portrait of a System With Repeated Zero Eigenvalue
questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-3x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-9x(t)+3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvector corresponding to the only eigenvalue $\lambda =0$ of the system's matrix $A$ is $v=[1,\text{ }3]^{T}.$ The vector $w={[-\frac{1}{3},\text{ }0]}^{T}$ is such that $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$  Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the system?

*Hint: Here, the dotted line represents the equilibrium solutions.*
questions.worked_solution:
Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =0$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $v,$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

In our case, 

$$
\lambda =0,\,v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t-\frac{1}{3} \\ 3t\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that ${x}_{E}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ are equilibrium solutions of the system since ${x}_{E}^{′}(t)=0.$ These solutions form the line with the equation $y=3x$ in the phase space, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14076166/assets/3a70188cf5de7e7b64530aa661447b7fa7fc1e918ca3de41088e67274d813b7a.png)

Now, we consider some general solutions of the form 

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t-\frac{1}{3} \\ 3t\end{aligned}].
$$

For example:

- When ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=3,$ we get the following curve: 

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=3t \\ y=9t+3\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add it to the phase space:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14076166/assets/37deb5a0fda7ef15a016ec2d73a3b935074b6696184dd480ebe5b858ce517500.png)

- When ${c}_{1}=-1$ and ${c}_{2}=-3,$ we get the following curve: 

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-3t \\ y=-9t-3\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add it to the phase space:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14076166/assets/60b49680cf94888122f25432586a3546dea206ae960f951afd187444afc8881a.png)

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14076166/assets/7b4de40b147f1745986476ab0b0cbad22ad0484924f62389c6c19187d5d06245.png)
